blocks.title: A cache keeps selected memory blocks close to the CPU
paragraphs: A cache stores copies of blocks identified by address information. The placement rule chooses a set, the tag identifies which block occupies a way, and the replacement rule chooses a victim when that set is full.
Our workspace is an initially empty read-only cache with allocation on every read miss and least-recently-used replacement. It does not silently assume write-policy behavior or model access latency.

blocks.title: Decompose an address without adding way bits
paragraphs: For eight-bit byte addresses, four-byte blocks, two sets and two ways, the offset has two bits, set index one bit and tag five bits. Ways are alternatives inside a set, not an additional address field. Data capacity is 4×2×2 = 16 bytes, excluding metadata.
Byte address 45 has block number floor(45/4)=11 and offset 1. Set = 11 mod 2 = 1; tag = floor(11/2)=5. Reconstruct the address as ((5×2)+1)×4+1 = 45.

blocks.title: A hit changes LRU order
paragraphs: Use the stated two-way cache and read byte addresses 0,8,0,16,8. All map to set 0 with tags 0,1,0,2,1. Starting empty, the results are miss, miss, hit, miss, miss.

Store tags from least to most recently used. After each access, set 0 is [0], [0,1], [1,0], [0,2], [2,1]. The hit on tag 0 makes tag 1 the next victim; treating a hit as no state change would implement the wrong replacement behavior.
Reads 0,1,3 share one four-byte block and therefore produce miss, hit, hit from an empty cache. Distinguish a byte change from a block change.

blocks.title: Explain a transformation through its access sequence
paragraphs: Temporal locality reuses recently accessed data; spatial locality accesses nearby addresses in the same or neighboring blocks. To justify a transformation, compare the actual access order, block mapping and live working set.

For row-major array storage, traversing adjacent elements of a row tends to use contiguous addresses. Changing traversal order or blocking a computation can improve reuse, but the benefit depends on dimensions, block size, associativity and competing data.
Do not promise a hit rate from the word “locality” alone. Trace a small representative case under the given cache and check that program dependencies and results are preserved.

blocks.title: Keep replacement and write decisions separate
paragraphs: LRU chooses the least recently accessed resident line. FIFO instead follows insertion order; a hit need not change that order. A task must state which policy to trace.

Write-through propagates writes toward the next level immediately under its protocol; write-back records a dirty cached copy for later writeback. Write allocation is a separate miss decision. The read-only workspace implements none of these write transitions, so write traces need an explicitly specified model.

blocks.title: Reconstruct addresses and retain exact state
paragraphs: Derive block, set, tag and offset; look up the tag only in its selected set; apply the declared replacement rule; and record every state change, including hits.
Use the cache workspace to step the controlled LRU trace. Practice offers address-field and hit/miss checks plus unscored optimization reasoning.

cards.prompt: Where do associativity bits appear in a cache address?
cards.answer: They do not form a separate address field. Address bits select block offset, set index and tag; ways are alternatives within the selected set.

cards.prompt: What data capacity has S sets, W ways and B-byte blocks?
cards.answer: S×W×B bytes, excluding tags and validity/replacement metadata. Be explicit whether a supplied capacity includes metadata.

cards.prompt: Does an LRU hit change replacement state?
cards.answer: Yes. Move the accessed line to most recently used. Otherwise a later victim can be wrong.

cards.prompt: Can different byte addresses hit the same cache line?
cards.answer: Yes, when they belong to the same memory block and that block is resident in its selected set. Their offsets differ while block identity stays the same.

cards.prompt: How should a cache optimization claim be justified?
cards.answer: Show the changed access order and resulting block reuse/conflicts under the stated cache, while preserving program results. Locality is not a guaranteed hit percentage.

cards.prompt: Are replacement policy and write policy the same choice?
cards.answer: No. Replacement selects a victim. Write-through/write-back and allocation decisions determine how writes propagate and whether a miss installs a line.

guided.title: Justify an access-order change
guided.prompt: A row-major array is traversed column by column. Explain when row-by-row traversal might reduce misses, and why it is not an unconditional guarantee.
rubric: Relate adjacent row elements to nearby addresses and spatial locality.
State dimensions, cache block size/capacity/associativity and other active data needed for a concrete trace.
Preserve program dependencies and results; compare actual block accesses rather than claiming a fixed improvement.
